Title: Too close? Give them room.
Caption:
Standing too close can make another child uncomfortable.

Step back and leave comfortable room. If they move away, respect the extra space.

Practice side by side with an adult: ask, “Is this enough room?” Then listen to the answer.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Personal space is part of kindness.
Caption: One friendship habit to practice: giving another child comfortable personal space. Model stepping back, asking whether there is enough room, and listening to the answer. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and the free parent activity at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: If they step back, give more room.
Caption: Instead of “Stop being annoying,” name the action: “Give them a little more room.” Practice calmly and adapt to the child. More adult-guided friendship practice in Social Skills Boot Camp, available through books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “Look at this!” Not in their face.
Caption:
Holding an object right in another child’s face can interrupt or overwhelm them.

Hold it at a comfortable distance. Ask if they want to see it, then wait.

Try: “Would you like to see my drawing?” If the answer is no, put it away and choose another moment.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Show your idea. Leave them space.
Caption: Excitement does not need to mean putting a toy or picture in someone’s face. Practice holding it back and asking, “Would you like to see?” Social Skills Boot Camp includes concrete habits to rehearse with an adult. Explore the books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “Want to see it?” Then wait.
Caption: A useful replacement for pushing an object toward a playmate: ask once, leave space, and wait for the answer. Try one small role-play together, then explore more friendship practice at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: A hug needs a yes.
Caption:
Touching someone without asking can cross their boundary, even when the intention is friendly.

Ask before touching and respect the answer. A wave or a hello can be enough.

Practice: “Would you like a hug?” If the answer is no, say, “Okay,” and offer a wave instead.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Friendliness does not require a hug.
Caption: Practice asking before touching, including friendly hugs. A child can respect someone else’s “no” and have their own “no” respected too. Explore adult-guided boundary practice in Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “No hug?” “Okay. I can wave.”
Caption: Try this role-play: “Would you like a hug?” “No thanks.” “Okay. I can wave.” Respecting the answer is the useful habit. Find the Social Skills Rules story and workbook at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Not your favorite? Don’t put it down.
Caption:
Calling another child’s favorite game stupid can shut down the conversation.

State your preference without insulting theirs. Ask what they like about it.

Try: “That game isn’t my favorite. What do you like about it?” You can be curious without pretending to agree.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: “Not for me” is not “That’s stupid.”
Caption: Your child does not have to like the same games or food as a friend. Practice expressing a preference without insulting someone else’s enjoyment. Explore Not Everyone Likes Pizza and Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Different favorites. Room for both.
Caption: A question to rehearse: “What do you like about it?” Curiosity can leave room for a conversation even when preferences differ. More parent-guided practice and the Social Skills Rules books: books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Before jumping in, wait for an opening.
Caption:
Starting a new story while someone is still speaking can take away their turn.

Pause until they finish, respond to what they said, and then ask for a turn.

Try: “That sounds fun. Can I tell you about my game?” Then wait for an answer.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: A pause can give someone a turn.
Caption: One habit to practice before the next conversation: wait until the other person finishes. Then respond to their topic before starting your own story. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “Can I tell you?” Wait for the answer.
Caption: Practice the ordinary-conversation script: “That sounds fun. Can I tell you about my game?” Urgent safety needs are different and deserve adult attention. Find more concrete friendship practice at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Always chasing the same friend?
Caption:
Repeatedly chasing someone who is not interested can leave a child hurt and frustrated.

Notice willing friends and put effort into relationships that go both ways.

Ask together: “Who seems glad to spend time with you? Who invites you to join?” Look at the pattern, not one missed invitation.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: One invitation does not define your child.
Caption: When a child feels excluded, start by listening. Then notice patterns of friendship that go both ways. Not Everyone Likes Pizza offers a Christian-perspective story for this conversation. Explore the story and companion workbook at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Look for friends who choose you too.
Caption: A useful question after repeated exclusion: “Who seems happy to spend time with you?” A missed invitation is not a verdict on a child’s worth. Explore Not Everyone Likes Pizza and its companion practice at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: They asked a question. Answer it first.
Caption:
Ignoring another child’s question and changing the subject can make the conversation feel one-sided.

Answer what was asked, add a related response, and leave room for another turn.

“What did you draw?” “I drew a cat. Do you like drawing animals?” Then listen.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: A question deserves room for an answer.
Caption: Practice one small conversation sequence: answer the question, add something related, then give the other person a turn. Adapt the communication method to the child. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Answer first. Then connect.
Caption: “What did you draw?” “A cat. Do you like drawing animals?” The point is shared participation, not a perfect memorized sentence. Try the free companion activity and explore the books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Only your favorite topic again?
Caption:
Returning every conversation to one favorite topic can leave little room for the other child.

Ask about their interest, listen to the answer, and respond before switching topics.

“You said you like dinosaurs. Which one is your favorite?” Listen first; you do not need to be an expert.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Try one question about their favorite.
Caption: Try one genuine question about the other child’s interests. Then listen and respond instead of immediately returning to a favorite topic. Social Skills Boot Camp offers concrete conversation practice. Explore it at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Curiosity is not a quiz. Listen too.
Caption: Friendship practice is not a question checklist. Model curiosity, a related response, and room for the answer. Find the free activity and the Social Skills Rules books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Want to join in? Ask. Then wait.
Caption:
Jumping into another child’s game without asking can interrupt what they are already doing.

Ask to join, wait for the answer, and learn the game’s rules if invited.

“Can I join?” If yes: “How are you playing?” If no: choose another safe activity.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: “Can I join?” Then give them time.
Caption: Practice joining a game before a difficult moment: “Can I join?” Wait for the answer. If invited, ask how the game works. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and its adult-guided activities at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: If you can join, learn their game.
Caption: A respectful way into a game starts with a question, not grabbing the pieces or changing the rules. Rehearse the words and the waiting together. More friendship practice: books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: They said no. Stop pushing.
Caption:
Arguing after someone declines a game or invitation can push the other person away.

Accept the answer and choose another option rather than trying to wear them down.

“Want to play?” “No thanks.” “Okay. I’ll try something else.” Practice both sides.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: “No thanks.” “Okay.”
Caption: A short role-play can make respecting “no” more concrete: ask, hear the answer, and practice “Okay.” The child’s own boundaries matter too. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: A boundary is not a debate to win.
Caption: Repeatedly asking after a refusal can turn an invitation into pressure. Practice choosing another safe activity or willing friend. Find adult-guided friendship activities and the books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “Only my game.” Try taking turns.
Caption:
Insisting on choosing every game can leave another child feeling that their preferences do not count.

Offer safe choices and take turns choosing together.

“We could play your game first, then mine.” Both people can say no to something unsafe or uncomfortable.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Their choice matters. So does yours.
Caption: Practice a small piece of flexible play: two safe choices and a turn for each person to choose. Flexibility does not mean accepting harm or ignoring boundaries. Explore the Social Skills Rules books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Take turns choosing a safe activity.
Caption: “We could try your game, then mine.” Model one concrete way to share decisions rather than saying only “Be flexible.” More adult-guided practice in Social Skills Boot Camp: books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Need help? Tell a trusted adult.
Caption:
Trying to police every small peer mistake can make play feel controlling.

Ask an adult for help with danger, threats, bullying, or a problem you cannot safely handle.

Practice saying what happened, who needs help, and what feels unsafe. Never keep an unsafe secret to avoid “tattling.”

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Safety concerns always deserve help.
Caption: Help children distinguish trying to control every small peer mistake from getting adult help with danger, bullying, or harm. When unsure, asking a trusted adult is okay. Explore Social Skills Boot Camp at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: Teach problem-solving, not silence.
Caption: Never use “Don’t tattle” to silence a safety concern. Practice explaining what happened and what help is needed. Find adult-guided social-skills discussion and the books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “Be good” is not a practice plan.
Caption:
Vague feedback can leave a child unsure which action to change.

Name one action and model a specific replacement. Then rehearse it together.

Instead of “Be nicer,” try “Wait until they finish. Then ask one related question.” Switch roles.

Explore Social Skills Boot Camp and Not Everyone Likes Pizza by Arianna Andersen at books.familygallerytv.com. Books are available on Amazon.

Title: Name the behavior. Not a label.
Caption: Give the child a useful next step, not a label. Model one action, switch roles, and notice a specific improvement. Social Skills Boot Camp makes everyday friendship habits concrete. Explore the books at books.familygallerytv.com.

Title: “You waited for the answer.”
Caption: “You waited for my answer” names a useful action more clearly than “Good job.” Start small and practice together. Explore the Social Skills Rules story, workbook, and free companion activity at books.familygallerytv.com.
